To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Cu and Ni emissions from the Harjavalat smelter resulted in a deficit in base cations (Ca, Mg, K) and a decrease in base saturation in the topmost soil layers.

(i) the accumulation of Cu and/or Ni in the organic layer of forest soils in the vicinity of Harjavalta smelter has resulted (ii) in a decrease in the availability of base cations in the organic layer, (iii) in an increase in exchangeable Cu and/or Ni, (iv) and in a decrease in BS.
The accumulation of Cu, Ni and Zn in forest soil close (1 km) to a Cu-Ni smelting complex in SW Finland has resulted in a significant reduction of the base saturation of the forest soil.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of heavy metals on the availability of macronutrients and on soil acidification.

(1) the effects of Cu- and Ni-contamination in the vicinity of a Cu-Ni smeltery on soil chemistry; (2) the effects of soil contamination on soil chemistry in the vicinity of other industrial plants; (3) the effects of heavy metal contamination of soil on the growth of forest plants.
the following questions: How does the accumulation of heavy metals affect nutrient availability and the cation exchange capacity of the forest soil in the area?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Cu and Ni contamination has resulted in a deficiency of base cations and BS in the organic layer of the forest soil in the immediate vicinity of the Cu-NI smelter at Harjavalla, SW Finland.
heavy metal pollution has resulted in a decrease of BS, but not in a decrease of pH or an increase of exchangeable acidity or Al in the organic layer.
the heavy-metal emissions have not caused a soil acidification in the vicinity of Harjavalta smelter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of heavy metal contamination in the vicinity of Harjavalta smelter are mainly restricted to the organic layer and that the soil pH, exchangeable Al and base saturation in the mineral soil are still within the limits of natural variation.
heavy-metal emissions from a Cu-Ni smelting plant can cause a deficit of base-cations in the forest soil and thus affect the availability of macronutrients.
heavy metal pollution has not resulted in any significant change in soil pH and exchangeable Al, but the base cation status of the organic layer has been severely impaired by Cu and Ni.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the heavy metals Cu and Ni are not likely to cause any major changes in forest soils in the vicinity of a Cu-Ni smelting facility.
the heavy metal contamination of forest soils can result in a deficit of macronutrients and a change in CEC and BS.
the use of the summation method to determine cation exchange capacity in forest soil is not recommended unless Cu and Ni cation concentrations are also included in calculations.
